{"name": "Sun: Extended Corona (F-corona / Outer):", "subtitle": "", "body": "Extended outer solar corona at ~50 solar radii (~0.23 AU).
F-corona (dust-scattered sunlight with Fraunhofer lines) dominates at this distance.

Layer hierarchy within this shell:
* Visible streamer belt: 4-6 R_sun (see Streamer Belt shell)
* Alfven surface (corona/solar wind boundary): ~15-20 R_sun (see Alfven Surface shell)
Parker Solar Probe first crossing: 18.8 R_sun, April 28, 2021
* F-corona (dust-scattered): 3-50+ R_sun -- this shell's extent

* Temperature: ~1-2 million K (coronal heating paradox)
* Beyond the Alfven surface, plasma is solar wind, not true corona
* Parker Solar Probe closest approach: ~8.8 R_sun (2024)
* Radiates at ~1.159 nm (extreme ultraviolet to X-ray)

MAPS C/2026 A1 entered SOHO/LASCO C3 field (~33 R_sun) on April 2, 2026,
already inside this shell and approaching the Alfven surface."}
text:
Sun: Extended Corona (F-corona / Outer):

Extended outer solar corona at ~50 solar radii (~0.23 AU).
F-corona (dust-scattered sunlight with Fraunhofer lines) dominates at this distance.

Layer hierarchy within this shell:
* Visible streamer belt: 4-6 R_sun (see Streamer Belt shell)
* Alfven surface (corona/solar wind boundary): ~15-20 R_sun (see Alfven Surface shell)
Parker Solar Probe first crossing: 18.8 R_sun, April 28, 2021
* F-corona (dust-scattered): 3-50+ R_sun -- this shell's extent

* Temperature: ~1-2 million K (coronal heating paradox)
* Beyond the Alfven surface, plasma is solar wind, not true corona
* Parker Solar Probe closest approach: ~8.8 R_sun (2024)
* Radiates at ~1.159 nm (extreme ultraviolet to X-ray)

MAPS C/2026 A1 entered SOHO/LASCO C3 field (~33 R_sun) on April 2, 2026,
already inside this shell and approaching the Alfven surface.

customdata:
{"name": "Sun: Roche Limit (Fluid Body / Comet):", "subtitle": "", "body": "The Roche limit marks where tidal forces overcome a body's self-gravity.
It is NOT absolute -- tensile strength can allow survival inside it.

Formula: d = 2.44 x R_sun x (rho_sun / rho_comet)^(1/3)
Solar density: 1,408 kg/m^3 | Comet density: ~500 kg/m^3
Result: ~3.45 R_sun (~0.016 AU) from Sun center

Key physics:
* Roche limit depends on DENSITY RATIO only -- not on nucleus mass or size
* Tensile strength can allow survival inside the limit:
Ikeya-Seki (~5 km) survived at 1.66 R_sun (0.008 AU)
Great Comet of 1843 survived at 1.19 R_sun (0.006 AU)
Lovejoy (C/2011 W3, ~500 m) survived briefly at ~1.2 R_sun
* Larger nuclei: stronger self-gravity + stronger material bonds

MAPS C/2026 A1 context:
* Disintegrated at 8.33 R_sun (0.039 AU) -- OUTSIDE the Roche limit
* Killed by thermal ablation and rotational spin-up, not tidal forces
* Debris swept through this shell to perihelion at 1.23 R_sun (0.006 AU)
* The nucleus never reached the Roche limit intact"}
text:
Sun: Roche Limit (Fluid Body / Comet):

The Roche limit marks where tidal forces overcome a body's self-gravity.
It is NOT absolute -- tensile strength can allow survival inside it.

Formula: d = 2.44 x R_sun x (rho_sun / rho_comet)^(1/3)
Solar density: 1,408 kg/m^3 | Comet density: ~500 kg/m^3
Result: ~3.45 R_sun (~0.016 AU) from Sun center

Key physics:
* Roche limit depends on DENSITY RATIO only -- not on nucleus mass or size
* Tensile strength can allow survival inside the limit:
Ikeya-Seki (~5 km) survived at 1.66 R_sun (0.008 AU)
Great Comet of 1843 survived at 1.19 R_sun (0.006 AU)
Lovejoy (C/2011 W3, ~500 m) survived briefly at ~1.2 R_sun
* Larger nuclei: stronger self-gravity + stronger material bonds

MAPS C/2026 A1 context:
* Disintegrated at 8.33 R_sun (0.039 AU) -- OUTSIDE the Roche limit
* Killed by thermal ablation and rotational spin-up, not tidal forces
* Debris swept through this shell to perihelion at 1.23 R_sun (0.006 AU)
* The nucleus never reached the Roche limit intact

customdata:
{"name": "Sun: Streamer Belt / Visible Corona:", "subtitle": "", "body": "The streamer belt is the brightest, most structured region of the visible solar corona,
extending from the inner corona out to about 4-6 solar radii. This is the corona that
observers see during total solar eclipses as a pearly white halo around the Sun.

Three components of white-light corona:
* K-corona (kontinuierlich): Sunlight scattered off free electrons. Dominates within 2-3 R_sun.
Spectrum is continuous -- electrons move too fast to preserve absorption lines.
* F-corona (Fraunhofer): Sunlight scattered off dust. Shows Fraunhofer absorption lines.
Dominates beyond ~3 R_sun, extends to ~15 R_sun. Has an oval shape.
* E-corona (emission): Line emission from ionized Fe, Ni, Ca. Visible to ~2 R_sun.

* Helmet streamers: Dense magnetic structures extending 4-6 R_sun. Source of slow solar wind.
* Temperature: ~1-2 million K

MAPS C/2026 A1 context:
MAPS was detected in SOHO/LASCO C3 (~33 R_sun field) from April 2, 2026.
It passed through this visible streamer belt on April 3-4 before perihelion."}
text:
Sun: Streamer Belt / Visible Corona:

The streamer belt is the brightest, most structured region of the visible solar corona,
extending from the inner corona out to about 4-6 solar radii. This is the corona that
observers see during total solar eclipses as a pearly white halo around the Sun.

Three components of white-light corona:
* K-corona (kontinuierlich): Sunlight scattered off free electrons. Dominates within 2-3 R_sun.
Spectrum is continuous -- electrons move too fast to preserve absorption lines.
* F-corona (Fraunhofer): Sunlight scattered off dust. Shows Fraunhofer absorption lines.
Dominates beyond ~3 R_sun, extends to ~15 R_sun. Has an oval shape.
* E-corona (emission): Line emission from ionized Fe, Ni, Ca. Visible to ~2 R_sun.

* Helmet streamers: Dense magnetic structures extending 4-6 R_sun. Source of slow solar wind.
* Temperature: ~1-2 million K

MAPS C/2026 A1 context:
MAPS was detected in SOHO/LASCO C3 (~33 R_sun field) from April 2, 2026.
It passed through this visible streamer belt on April 3-4 before perihelion.

customdata:
{"name": "Sun: Alfven Surface:", "subtitle": "", "body": "The true outer boundary of the solar corona. Beyond this point, plasma can no longer
communicate back to the Sun -- the corona becomes the solar wind.

* Measured directly: Parker Solar Probe, April 28, 2021 at 18.8 R_sun (13 million km)
First spacecraft to enter the corona -- 'touching the Sun' for ~5 hours.
* Not a smooth sphere: spikes and valleys from solar magnetic activity.
Polar coronal holes: ~12-15 R_sun | Streamer belt: ~17-19 R_sun

Why it matters:
* Inside: plasma magnetically connected to the Sun. Alfven waves propagate inward.
* Outside: solar wind -- causally disconnected, flowing outward at 300-800 km/s.
* Governs the Sun's angular momentum loss and spin-down rate over billions of years.

MAPS C/2026 A1 context:
* MAPS crossed inward ~April 3, 18:00 UTC -- ~20 hours before disintegration.
* Inside this surface the comet was in magnetically connected 1-2 million K plasma.
* The corona paradox: hotter farther from surface -- still unexplained (Alfven waves,
nanoflares, and magnetic reconnection are leading candidate mechanisms)."}
text:
Sun: Alfven Surface:

The true outer boundary of the solar corona. Beyond this point, plasma can no longer
communicate back to the Sun -- the corona becomes the solar wind.

* Measured directly: Parker Solar Probe, April 28, 2021 at 18.8 R_sun (13 million km)
First spacecraft to enter the corona -- 'touching the Sun' for ~5 hours.
* Not a smooth sphere: spikes and valleys from solar magnetic activity.
Polar coronal holes: ~12-15 R_sun | Streamer belt: ~17-19 R_sun

Why it matters:
* Inside: plasma magnetically connected to the Sun. Alfven waves propagate inward.
* Outside: solar wind -- causally disconnected, flowing outward at 300-800 km/s.
* Governs the Sun's angular momentum loss and spin-down rate over billions of years.

MAPS C/2026 A1 context:
* MAPS crossed inward ~April 3, 18:00 UTC -- ~20 hours before disintegration.
* Inside this surface the comet was in magnetically connected 1-2 million K plasma.
* The corona paradox: hotter farther from surface -- still unexplained (Alfven waves,
nanoflares, and magnetic reconnection are leading candidate mechanisms).

customdata:
{"name": "Sun: Inner Corona (K-corona):", "subtitle": "", "body": "The solar inner corona closest to the surface. Dominated by the K-corona --
sunlight scattered off free electrons. Extends to ~2-3 solar radii.

* Temperature: 1-3 million K (increases with altitude -- the coronal heating paradox)
* K-corona dominates within ~2.3 R_sun; F-corona (dust) takes over beyond ~3 R_sun
* Density: much denser than outer corona, but still far less than photosphere
* Magnetic structures: coronal loops, coronal holes, streamers
* Solar flares and CMEs originate here

Roche limit proximity:
* The fluid Roche limit for comets (~3.45 R_sun) lies just outside this shell.
* Any Kreutz sungrazer penetrating the inner K-corona is at or inside the tidal
disruption threshold. MAPS C/2026 A1 perihelion reached 1.23 R_sun --
deep inside both the inner corona and the Roche limit simultaneously.

* Solar Inner Corona (extends to 2-3 solar radii, ~0.014 AU)
* Temperature: 1-2M K, or an average of about 1.5M K
* Radiates at an average wavelength of 1.93 nm, extreme ultraviolet to soft X-ray."}
text:
Sun: Inner Corona (K-corona):

The solar inner corona closest to the surface. Dominated by the K-corona --
sunlight scattered off free electrons. Extends to ~2-3 solar radii.

* Temperature: 1-3 million K (increases with altitude -- the coronal heating paradox)
* K-corona dominates within ~2.3 R_sun; F-corona (dust) takes over beyond ~3 R_sun
* Density: much denser than outer corona, but still far less than photosphere
* Magnetic structures: coronal loops, coronal holes, streamers
* Solar flares and CMEs originate here

Roche limit proximity:
* The fluid Roche limit for comets (~3.45 R_sun) lies just outside this shell.
* Any Kreutz sungrazer penetrating the inner K-corona is at or inside the tidal
disruption threshold. MAPS C/2026 A1 perihelion reached 1.23 R_sun --
deep inside both the inner corona and the Roche limit simultaneously.

* Solar Inner Corona (extends to 2-3 solar radii, ~0.014 AU)
* Temperature: 1-2M K, or an average of about 1.5M K
* Radiates at an average wavelength of 1.93 nm, extreme ultraviolet to soft X-ray.

customdata:
{"name": "Sun: Chromosphere:", "subtitle": "", "body": "The chromosphere is a dynamic and visually stunning layer of the Sun's atmosphere, sandwiched between the
photosphere (the visible surface) and the corona (the outermost layer). It's a region of dramatic temperature
changes, intricate structures, and energetic events.

* The chromosphere is relatively thin, extending only about 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) above the photosphere.
It's also much less dense than the photosphere.
* The temperature in the chromosphere increases dramatically with altitude, from around 4,000 Kelvin at the
photosphere to about 20,000 Kelvin at the inner corona.
* The chromosphere gets its name from the Greek word \"chroma,\" meaning color, because of its reddish appearance.
This color is primarily due to the strong emission of light from hydrogen atoms
* The chromosphere is a constantly changing environment, with a variety of features that evolve and erupt on
different timescales:
* Spicules: These are jet-like eruptions of plasma that rise and fall like geysers, covering the chromosphere
in a dynamic, \"grass-like\" pattern.
* Filaments and prominences: These are large, cool, dense structures of plasma suspended in the chromosphere
and corona by magnetic fields. When seen against the bright disk of the Sun, they appear as dark filaments.
When seen extending beyond the Sun's edge, they appear as bright prominences.
* Plages: These are bright regions in the chromosphere associated with active regions, where magnetic fields
are concentrated.

* Radius: from Photosphere to 1.5 Solar radii or ~0.00465 - 0.0070 AU
* Temperature: ~6,000 to 20,000 K, for a average of 10,000 K
* Radiates at an average peak wavelength of ~290 nm, ultraviolet range, invisible."}
text:
Sun: Chromosphere:

The chromosphere is a dynamic and visually stunning layer of the Sun's atmosphere, sandwiched between the
photosphere (the visible surface) and the corona (the outermost layer). It's a region of dramatic temperature
changes, intricate structures, and energetic events.

* The chromosphere is relatively thin, extending only about 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) above the photosphere.
It's also much less dense than the photosphere.
* The temperature in the chromosphere increases dramatically with altitude, from around 4,000 Kelvin at the
photosphere to about 20,000 Kelvin at the inner corona.
* The chromosphere gets its name from the Greek word "chroma," meaning color, because of its reddish appearance.
This color is primarily due to the strong emission of light from hydrogen atoms
* The chromosphere is a constantly changing environment, with a variety of features that evolve and erupt on
different timescales:
* Spicules: These are jet-like eruptions of plasma that rise and fall like geysers, covering the chromosphere
in a dynamic, "grass-like" pattern.
* Filaments and prominences: These are large, cool, dense structures of plasma suspended in the chromosphere
and corona by magnetic fields. When seen against the bright disk of the Sun, they appear as dark filaments.
When seen extending beyond the Sun's edge, they appear as bright prominences.
* Plages: These are bright regions in the chromosphere associated with active regions, where magnetic fields
are concentrated.

* Radius: from Photosphere to 1.5 Solar radii or ~0.00465 - 0.0070 AU
* Temperature: ~6,000 to 20,000 K, for a average of 10,000 K
* Radiates at an average peak wavelength of ~290 nm, ultraviolet range, invisible.

customdata:
{"name": "Sun: Photosphere", "subtitle": "", "body": "Solar Convective Zone and Photosphere, the visible surface.
* The photosphere is the visible surface of the Sun. It's a relatively thin layer, only about 500 kilometers thick.
* Including both the Convective Zone and the Photosphere, the radius is from 0.7 to 1 Solar radii, or about 0.00465 AU.
* Temperature: from 2M K at the Radiative Zone to ~5,500K at the Photosphere.
* Convection transports energy to the visible \"surface\" of the Sun. The convection process starts at the Radiative Zone
* At the Photosphere, the energy is radiated as visible light. Radiation emits at a peak wavelength at 527.32 nm, which
is in the green spectrum. The Sun's emitted light is a combination of all visible wavelengths, resulting in a yellowish-white color.

* The photosphere is cooler than the Sun's core and the layers above it, but still hot enough to make the photosphere glow brightly.
* To the naked eye, the photosphere appears as a smooth, yellow disk. However, closer observations reveal a variety of features, including:
* Granulation: This is a pattern of small, bright cells surrounded by darker boundaries, caused by convection
currents bringing hot plasma up from the Sun's interior.
* Sunspots: These are dark, cooler regions on the photosphere caused by strong magnetic fields. They can be
larger than Earth and last for days or weeks.
* Faculae: These are bright regions surrounding sunspots, also associated with magnetic fields.
* Energy transport: The photosphere is where the Sun's energy, generated in its core through nuclear fusion,
is finally released as light. This energy has traveled outward through the Sun's interior in the form of
radiation and convection, and it's in the photosphere that it transitions to primarily radiation, allowing it
to escape into space.
* Spectrum: The photosphere emits a continuous spectrum of light, which includes all colors of the rainbow.
* Solar activity: The photosphere is also where many solar activity events originate, such as:
* Solar flares: These are sudden, intense bursts of energy and radiation caused by the release of magnetic
energy in the solar atmosphere.
* Coronal mass ejections (CMEs): These are massive eruptions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun's corona,
often associated with flares.
* Solar activity events originating in the photosphere can affect Earth's magnetic field and disrupt satellites,
communication systems, and power grids."}
text:
Sun: Photosphere

Solar Convective Zone and Photosphere, the visible surface.
* The photosphere is the visible surface of the Sun. It's a relatively thin layer, only about 500 kilometers thick.
* Including both the Convective Zone and the Photosphere, the radius is from 0.7 to 1 Solar radii, or about 0.00465 AU.
* Temperature: from 2M K at the Radiative Zone to ~5,500K at the Photosphere.
* Convection transports energy to the visible "surface" of the Sun. The convection process starts at the Radiative Zone
* At the Photosphere, the energy is radiated as visible light. Radiation emits at a peak wavelength at 527.32 nm, which
is in the green spectrum. The Sun's emitted light is a combination of all visible wavelengths, resulting in a yellowish-white color.

* The photosphere is cooler than the Sun's core and the layers above it, but still hot enough to make the photosphere glow brightly.
* To the naked eye, the photosphere appears as a smooth, yellow disk. However, closer observations reveal a variety of features, including:
* Granulation: This is a pattern of small, bright cells surrounded by darker boundaries, caused by convection
currents bringing hot plasma up from the Sun's interior.
* Sunspots: These are dark, cooler regions on the photosphere caused by strong magnetic fields. They can be
larger than Earth and last for days or weeks.
* Faculae: These are bright regions surrounding sunspots, also associated with magnetic fields.
* Energy transport: The photosphere is where the Sun's energy, generated in its core through nuclear fusion,
is finally released as light. This energy has traveled outward through the Sun's interior in the form of
radiation and convection, and it's in the photosphere that it transitions to primarily radiation, allowing it
to escape into space.
* Spectrum: The photosphere emits a continuous spectrum of light, which includes all colors of the rainbow.
* Solar activity: The photosphere is also where many solar activity events originate, such as:
* Solar flares: These are sudden, intense bursts of energy and radiation caused by the release of magnetic
energy in the solar atmosphere.
* Coronal mass ejections (CMEs): These are massive eruptions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun's corona,
often associated with flares.
* Solar activity events originating in the photosphere can affect Earth's magnetic field and disrupt satellites,
communication systems, and power grids.

{"name": "MAPS (C/2026 A1) \u2014 Nucleus Disintegrated", "subtitle": "", "body": "April 4, 2026 ~08:15 UTC | ~6 hours before perihelion
Position at disintegration:
Distance from Sun center: 0.039424 AU (5,897,801 km)
Distance from photosphere: 5,202,101 km (0.034774 AU) = 8.48 R_sun
Layer: between Alfven Surface (~18.8 R_sun, ~0.087 AU) and Streamer Belt (~6.0 R_sun, ~0.028 AU)
Solar environment:
Corona temperature at this distance: ~1-2 million K
Inside Alfven surface (crossed ~April 3 18:00 UTC): YES
Inside Streamer Belt (~6.0 R_sun, ~0.028 AU): NO -- died before reaching it
Inside Roche limit (~3.45 R_sun, ~0.016 AU): NO -- 3,497,636 km outside
Inside Inner K-corona (~3.0 R_sun, ~0.014 AU): NO
Physics of destruction (at 8.3 R_sun, ~0.039 AU):
Primary mechanisms at this distance:
1. Thermal ablation: 1-2 million K corona vaporizes surface ices
2. Rotational spin-up: outgassing jets torque the 400 m nucleus to breakup (only meters of surface loss needed)
Note: Tidal disruption requires being inside the Roche limit (~3.45 R_sun, ~0.016 AU). MAPS never reached it intact.
The Roche limit, inner K-corona, and perihelion were all crossed by debris only.
The ghost comet:
After disintegration, the debris swept inbound through the Streamer Belt, Roche limit, and inner K-corona as a headless
dust/ion cloud, reaching perihelion at 1.23 R_sun (0.006 AU) at 556 km/s. Then outbound: SOHO/LASCO tracked the fading debris
trail for ~36-40 hours, until ~April 6 01:00 UTC, by which point the cloud had dispersed to ~28 R_sun (~0.132 AU)
Peak brightness: magnitude -0.6 (SOHO/CCOR-1, moments before breakup)
Nucleus: ~400 m diameter (JWST March 2026)
Perihelion (6h later, debris only): 0.006 AU = 1.23 R_sun = 161,000 km from photosphere -- deep inside Roche limit and inner
K-corona as dust. Possibly last seen intact as the Great Comet of 363 AD -- 1,663 years ago."}

MAPS (C/2026 A1) — Nucleus Disintegrated
April 4, 2026 ~08:15 UTC | ~6 hours before perihelion
Position at disintegration:
Distance from Sun center: 0.039424 AU (5,897,801 km)
Distance from photosphere: 5,202,101 km (0.034774 AU) = 8.48 R_sun
Layer: between Alfven Surface (~18.8 R_sun, ~0.087 AU) and Streamer Belt (~6.0 R_sun, ~0.028 AU)
Solar environment:
Corona temperature at this distance: ~1-2 million K
Inside Alfven surface (crossed ~April 3 18:00 UTC): YES
Inside Streamer Belt (~6.0 R_sun, ~0.028 AU): NO -- died before reaching it
Inside Roche limit (~3.45 R_sun, ~0.016 AU): NO -- 3,497,636 km outside
Inside Inner K-corona (~3.0 R_sun, ~0.014 AU): NO
Physics of destruction (at 8.3 R_sun, ~0.039 AU):
Primary mechanisms at this distance:
1. Thermal ablation: 1-2 million K corona vaporizes surface ices
2. Rotational spin-up: outgassing jets torque the 400 m nucleus to breakup (only meters of surface loss needed)
Note: Tidal disruption requires being inside the Roche limit (~3.45 R_sun, ~0.016 AU). MAPS never reached it intact.
The Roche limit, inner K-corona, and perihelion were all crossed by debris only.
The ghost comet:
After disintegration, the debris swept inbound through the Streamer Belt, Roche limit, and inner K-corona as a headless
dust/ion cloud, reaching perihelion at 1.23 R_sun (0.006 AU) at 556 km/s. Then outbound: SOHO/LASCO tracked the fading debris
trail for ~36-40 hours, until ~April 6 01:00 UTC, by which point the cloud had dispersed to ~28 R_sun (~0.132 AU)
Peak brightness: magnitude -0.6 (SOHO/CCOR-1, moments before breakup)
Nucleus: ~400 m diameter (JWST March 2026)
Perihelion (6h later, debris only): 0.006 AU = 1.23 R_sun = 161,000 km from photosphere -- deep inside Roche limit and inner
K-corona as dust. Possibly last seen intact as the Great Comet of 363 AD -- 1,663 years ago.

{"name": "MAPS: Ghost Tail (debris arc)", "subtitle": "", "body": "April 4 08:15 UTC to April 6 01:00 UTC (~40 hours)
After disintegration at ~8.33 R_sun (~0.039 AU), debris swept
inbound through Streamer Belt (6 R_sun, 0.028 AU),
Roche limit (3.45 R_sun, 0.016 AU), inner K-corona (3.0 R_sun, 0.014 AU),
and perihelion (1.23 R_sun, 0.006 AU) at 556 km/s. Then outbound
until dispersed to ~29 R_sun (~0.132 AU) by April 6.
SOHO/LASCO tracked ~40h; no ground-based visibility.
The nucleus never reached any inner shell intact -- only this debris did.
Opacity fades from disintegration point toward April 6 dispersal."}
text:
MAPS: Ghost Tail (debris arc)
April 4 08:15 UTC to April 6 01:00 UTC (~40 hours)
After disintegration at ~8.33 R_sun (~0.039 AU), debris swept
inbound through Streamer Belt (6 R_sun, 0.028 AU),
Roche limit (3.45 R_sun, 0.016 AU), inner K-corona (3.0 R_sun, 0.014 AU),
and perihelion (1.23 R_sun, 0.006 AU) at 556 km/s. Then outbound
until dispersed to ~29 R_sun (~0.132 AU) by April 6.
SOHO/LASCO tracked ~40h; no ground-based visibility.
The nucleus never reached any inner shell intact -- only this debris did.
Opacity fades from disintegration point toward April 6 dispersal.

data.name: MAPS: Nucleus
text:
Nucleus of MAPS
Approximate size: 0.4 km
Cometary nuclei are 'dirty snowballs' - irregular chunks of ice, rock, and dust.
As they approach the Sun, surface ice sublimates, releasing gas and dust.
Note: The nucleus is far too small to show at scale with the coma.

_encyclopedia.MAPS:
Horizons: C/2026 A1. Comet MAPS (C/2026 A1) was a Kreutz sungrazer discovered January 13, 2026
from the AMACS1 Observatory in the Atacama Desert, Chile, by Maury, Attard, Parrott and Signoret.
It holds the record as the most distant Kreutz sungrazer ever detected at discovery -- found
81 days before perihelion, giving astronomers an unprecedented window of observation.

Paloma's Orrery began tracking this object under provisional designation 6AC4721
within days of its discovery, before JPL formally assigned it the Horizons ID C/2026 A1.
The orbital elements were sourced from MPEC 2026-A49 and integrated manually into the
Orrery's idealized orbit pipeline -- a rare case of tracking a comet from near-discovery
all the way through perihelion, disintegration, and the ghost outbound arc.

Orbital history:
* ~1,695-year orbital period: likely a second-generation fragment of the Great Comet of 371 BC.
* Possibly one of the daylight comets of 363 AD witnessed by Ammianus Marcellinus.
* Traveled from aphelion beyond 100 AU, inbound for over a millennium, to die in the corona.

Pre-perihelion observations:
* Nucleus: ~400 m diameter (JWST, March 2026) -- same size class as C/2011 W3 (Lovejoy).
* Blue-green coma (C2 Swan band emission) observed March 14, 2026 with 25-arcmin tail.
* Brightened 1.5 magnitudes in 3 days (March 6-9); activity plateaued March 11-17.

Final passage -- an experimental probe into the solar atmosphere:
* April 2: entered SOHO/LASCO C3 field (~33 R_sun, ~0.153 AU);
  crossed the extended F-corona. Visible in coronagraphs.
* April 3 ~18:00 UTC: crossed the Alfven surface (~18.8 R_sun, ~0.087 AU) --
  now inside the true corona; plasma magnetically connected to the Sun;
  immersed in 1-2 million K coronal plasma.
* April 4 ~08:15 UTC: NUCLEUS DISINTEGRATED at ~8.33 R_sun (~0.039 AU).
  Between the Alfven surface and the Streamer Belt. OUTSIDE the Roche limit,
  Streamer Belt, and inner K-corona -- thermal ablation and rotational spin-up
  killed it before tidal forces had a chance to act.
  Peak brightness: magnitude -0.6 (SOHO/CCOR-1).
* April 4 ~14:22 UTC: the debris cloud reached perihelion at 1.23 R_sun
  (0.006 AU, 161,000 km from photosphere), velocity 556 km/s. It crossed
  the Streamer Belt (6 R_sun, 0.028 AU), Roche limit (3.45 R_sun, 0.016 AU),
  and inner K-corona (3.0 R_sun, 0.014 AU) as debris only. The nucleus
  never reached any of these shells intact.
* April 4-6: ghost comet outbound. SOHO/LASCO tracked the fading debris
  trail for ~36-40 hours. By April 6 ~01:00 UTC the cloud had dispersed
  to ~28 R_sun (~0.132 AU). Too diffuse for any ground-based detection.
  No naked-eye or amateur telescope visibility. The show was over.

No spacecraft has ever reached 1.23 solar radii. Parker Solar Probe's
closest approach is 8.8 R_sun (0.041 AU). MAPS disintegrated at 8.33 R_sun
(0.039 AU) -- slightly closer than Parker's best. The debris went deeper.

The orbit trace is the debris trail. The disintegration marker (green diamond)
marks the moment the nucleus was lost. The outbound arc is the ghost.

Module updated: April 2026 with Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6. In memoriam C/2026 A1.
